A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same CholecTrack20 dataset and tracking formalization. Text, tables, figures, and end matter support comparison despite extensive restructuring. Neither supplied PDF contains a separate appendix.

before.justification: v1 reports original dataset statistics, trajectory and label-correlation analyses, annotation-agreement measurements, and expert-mediated annotation corrections.

after.justification: v2 retains original dataset analyses and annotation-validation results and adds quantitative detection and tracking benchmarks in Tables 2–3 and Figures 8–10.

M1.justification: The annotation framework, class/operator-based identities, three trajectory perspectives, and two-second visibility tolerance remain substantively unchanged. v2 benchmarks existing detectors and trackers without introducing a new tracking algorithm or demonstrating a changed dataset-generation procedure.

E1.justification: The same 20-video laparoscopic dataset, seven tool categories, and three tracking perspectives are retained. v2 adds an explicitly evaluated tool-detection task in Section 4.1. Other datasets listed in its comparison table are contextual references, not additional experimental datasets.

E2.justification: v1 contains no model benchmark comparisons and refers readers to an accompanying paper. v2 Table 2 evaluates 13 detectors, including Faster-RCNN and YOLOv7–10. Table 3 evaluates six trackers across all three perspectives and additionally includes SORT for visibility tracking.

E3.justification: v2 introduces concrete benchmark protocols: COCO AP at multiple IoU thresholds, tracking reported at 25 FPS, HOTA, CLEAR and identity metrics, detection/identity counts, and inference speed. v1 primarily recommends TrackEval. The stated procedure-level 5:1:4 dataset split remains unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 adds model-performance analyses across trajectory perspectives, tool categories, visual challenges, and surgical phases (Tables 2–3; Figures 8–10). The original trajectory/correlation analyses remain in Figures 5–7, while v1's detailed annotation-validation confusion matrices are removed.

E5.justification: Both versions retain Jaccard/Cohen's Kappa annotation-agreement reporting and the 20-image inter-rater sample. Neither reports training-seed counts, repeated training runs, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The new benchmark displays report point estimates.

E6.justification: v2 adds extensive benchmark results absent from v1. Table 2 reports YOLOv9 AP at IoU 0.5:0.95 of 56.5%; Table 3 reports BoT-SORT HOTA of 17.4%, 27.0%, and 44.7% for intraoperative, intracorporeal, and visibility tracking. These are new results, not measured improvements over v1. Aggregate annotation-agreement scores remain unchanged.

T1.justification: The trajectory definitions and association-matrix formulation remain substantively equivalent. v2 condenses v1's identity-reassignment equation and surrounding definitions into prose in Section 3.2; no substantive new mathematical assumption, derivation, theorem, or proof is introduced.

C1.justification: The dataset and multi-perspective contribution are retained, but v2 elevates detector/tracker benchmarking and performance diagnostics into explicit main contributions. Its abstract additionally claims that existing methods achieve below 45% HOTA and lack accuracy for clinical translation, extending v1's dataset-centered claims.

C2.justification: Sections 4.1–4.3 add explanations involving tool similarity, re-identification, specimen-bag deformation, and visual challenges, plus calls for context-aware tracking and clinical applicability limitations. Some interpretations conflict with the evidence: the prose calls intracorporeal tracking hardest, whereas Table 3 consistently reports lower HOTA for intraoperative tracking.

D1.justification: v2 removes substantial usage documentation: the directory/JSON specification, conversion/visualization/loading script descriptions, named annotation systems, and guidance about overlapping source datasets. It adds benchmark implementation information, including pycocotools and the GPU used for speed measurements, and explicitly advertises dataset download availability.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands coverage of general object detection, tracking, and evaluation methods, including modern YOLO variants, BoT-SORT, FairMOT, and HOTA. Its dedicated Related Works section and dataset-comparison table broaden the research positioning beyond v1's primarily surgical background.

P1.justification: The title changes and much of the existing prose is rewritten and compressed. v1's Methods, Data Records, Technical Validation, Usage Notes, and Code Availability organization becomes a numbered conference-paper structure with consolidated methodology, separate related work, experiments, limitations, and conclusion.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a two-column layout, introduces a new clinical overview diagram, revises annotated-image examples, and converts dataset-statistics tables into Figure 4. It adds dataset/benchmark tables and performance plots, retains smaller versions of the trajectory plots, and removes the file-structure and validation-confusion-matrix figures.

improvement.justification: v2 supplies useful detector/tracker reference results and diagnostic analyses that v1 defers to another paper, improving empirical usefulness. However, it loses practical schema/code-use documentation and introduces consequential prose/table inconsistencies: YOLOv7 is called best despite YOLOv9's higher overall AP, and trajectory difficulty is misranked. These drawbacks limit the net quality gain.
